segments.say: Let's slow the experiment down until you can see the separate steps. Someone reads a list, you listen, and then you write what you remember. A word appears on your page. The interesting question is whether it arrived through your ears, or found its way there without ever being spoken.

There is an obvious possibility to check before calling this a memory error. Perhaps the supposedly missing word really was tucked into the reading somewhere. Perhaps you simply missed the moment when it appeared. Keep that question beside us while we look at what the researchers actually asked people to do.

In the experiment published by Henry Roediger and Kathleen McDermott in 1995, 36 Rice University undergraduates heard related word lists and completed memory tests. The setting was a university class. You can picture the task without picturing anything mysterious: listening to ordinary vocabulary, then trying to put the words back on paper.

Before we follow the students, it helps to separate two requests that sound almost interchangeable in everyday conversation. Tell me what you heard is one request. Tell me whether you heard this particular word is another. Both concern memory, but the answer begins in a different place in each task.

show.title: Two different tasks
items: Judge words shown on a test

segments.say: Imagine an empty answer page in front of you. There is no printed menu of possible words. To answer, you have to supply a word yourself. You might begin with something you can still almost hear, then search for another item, and another, until nothing else seems available to write.

Now imagine that the page already offers a word and asks whether it appeared earlier. You do not have to produce that candidate. It is sitting there, waiting for a judgment. Saying yes to a supplied word and writing an absent word yourself are different observations, even when the word is identical.

The order gives our question somewhere firm to stand. In this experiment, written recall came before the later recognition test. So when we examine an absent word appearing during recall, we should not imagine a student merely selecting it from that later sheet. That sheet had not supplied the answer yet.

Let the blank booklet stand for that first task. It has room for correct words, forgotten spaces, and possible additions, but it does not tell the listener what belongs there. The student has to decide which words to put down. That distinction will keep the later result from becoming a vaguer story about agreeing with suggestions.

The lists were built around related vocabulary, with a central associate left out. For the moment, we can leave the explanation of those relationships aside. What matters is a very literal boundary. A word could fit the company of the list beautifully and still not have been one of the words read aloud.

Suppose you were checking a remembered shopping list. An item could belong in the same cupboard as everything you heard, yet still be an addition. That is only an everyday comparison, not another experiment. It helps us preserve the difference between a sensible answer and an answer that matches the original wording.

If someone asks for the exact items, a related extra item does not become correct because it would have been useful. You can understand why it belongs without establishing that it was mentioned. In the word-list experiment, that same distinction makes the absent associate interesting: its suitability cannot settle its history.

The students were asked to write remembered words immediately after each list, and were instructed not to guess. That last detail matters to the story we tell. We should picture an attempt to report the reading, rather than a creative exercise in supplying every word that might match its general theme.

show.text: they were told not to guess

segments.say: An instruction cannot let us look directly inside another person's experience. What we can inspect is the answer they supplied and whether it matches what was presented. That gives us a response to check, rather than a complete account of the student's thoughts. We can call a response incorrect without pretending we have watched every thought that led to it.

This is a narrow comparison, almost like placing a transcript beside an answer sheet. Does this reported word occur in the material the student heard? A sensible, elegant, or closely related answer can still differ from the reading. For scoring that response, we need to know whether it was actually there.

show.title: What counts as an error here
items: That word was absent from the reading

segments.say: The omitted associate was written down on 40% of the lists. Notice what that percentage describes: occurrences across the list-recall task. It does not say that 40% of everything the students remembered was false. Holding onto the denominator keeps a striking result from quietly growing into a much larger claim.

Nor does that result tell you what would happen to every listener on every list. It describes the responses obtained in this experiment. You can let it be surprising without turning it into a prediction about your next conversation, your whole memory, or the listening exercise we began with earlier.
For comparison, the average recall rate for presented words was 65%. These rates describe different kinds of items. Correct recall and this specific error appeared within the same task.

There is something useful about allowing both observations to stay visible. You do not have to choose between describing the students as remembering or describing them as making an error. A page can contain accurate answers alongside an addition. Looking at each response is more informative than giving the entire person a label.

The result is already interesting at its actual size. A deliberately absent word sometimes appeared among the written answers. That finding sits alongside correct recall, and it describes a pattern across responses rather than an identical experience for every listener. Its surprise comes from the particular addition, not from a total failure to remember.

show.title: The finding at its actual size

segments.say: After the listening and recall sequence, the task changed. The students received a recognition test containing both presented and unpresented words. Now a candidate could arrive from the page itself. The question was no longer simply what they could produce, but how they would judge a word placed in front of them.

There are two different moments in that situation. You are certainly seeing the test word now. What you must decide is whether it also belonged to the earlier reading. The certainty of the present encounter does not answer the question about the earlier one.

We will look more closely at recognition judgments later. For now, the essential distinction is enough. An absent word written during free recall was supplied by the participant; an absent word accepted on the recognition test was supplied by the test. Both can be errors, but they are not the same kind of response.

There is also a reason to resist treating the later test as a completely fresh beginning. The students had already attempted recall. Their recognition answers came after that experience. The paper itself notes this limitation: prior recall could have influenced the later judgments.

Now we can return to the possibility we set aside. Was the missing word secretly presented? We need to specify when. It appeared later as a recognition-test candidate, but it was absent from the original reading. Appearing on a later sheet cannot put it back into an earlier spoken list.

show.title: The question we kept
items: Did it appear later on the test?

segments.say: That resolves the apparent trick. The finding does not depend on a whispered extra item hidden inside the presentation. In the reported procedure, the critical associate was omitted. When it appeared in immediate recall, the answer sheet contained a word that the reading had not supplied, before the recognition test offered it.

This is why a simple word task can be so revealing. There is a defined set of presented items to compare with the response. Unlike an entire afternoon or a disputed conversation, the original material is available for a direct check. The question concerns one word and one reading.

But identifying the mismatch is not the same as explaining how it happened. The written word tells us what the student reported. By itself, it does not tell us exactly when that word first came to mind, or which process made it seem eligible for the answer page. That is the next question.

show.cap: What we still do not know
show.sub: A response is not an explanation

segments.say: Imagine finding an extra puzzle piece on the table. First you establish that it does not belong to the original set. Then you ask how it arrived. Here, the equivalent puzzle is unusually specific: why should a particular related word find its way into recall, rather than just any word at all?

show.title: From the result to the explanation

segments.say: To explore that, we can turn back toward the words that really were spoken. Their relationship to the missing associate was part of the list design. The absence answers whether the word was presented; the relationships give us a place to investigate why it might nevertheless become a candidate for remembering.
